declarations.documentation:
One attachment a message carries, as Gmail describes it: the @filename@ the sender gave it ("" when it
has none, which an inline image often does), the @content_type@ the mail declares for it (e.g.
"application/pdf", "image/png"), the @size@ in bytes Gmail estimates for it, and the @attachment_id@
that `fetch_attachment` fetches it by — together with the MESSAGE's id, since an attachment id names a
part of one particular message. Plain data: knowing an attachment exists is one thing, and asking for its
bytes is another (`fetch_attachment`), so a mail can be read and judged without downloading anything.
Every part whose bytes Gmail holds behind an `attachmentId` is listed, which puts a mail's INLINE images
(the logo in an HTML signature) in the list beside its real files — the mail declares no difference
between them, so the list reports what is there and leaves what is worth fetching to its reader.

declarations.documentation:
A message's body as read: the @text@ itself, and the @content_type@ of the part that text came from —
"text/plain" for an ordinary mail, "text/html" when the message had no plain-text part (@text@ is then
MARKUP, tags and all), or `null` when it had neither and @text@ is Gmail's short SNIPPET preview rather
than a body at all. The type is a FIELD, not a sentence prefixed to the text: an announcement written into
the prose would fix one consumer's presentation inside this package, where nobody can inspect or override
it and every other consumer has to parse it back out — a reader that wants to strip the tags, or render
the markup, or ignore the distinction entirely needs the type as data. ABSENCE IS `null`, not `""`: a
media type is a string, so an empty one is a string a broken server could actually send, and the two
readings are told apart by the type rather than by a convention a reader has to know.

declarations.documentation:
Get a usable Google access token, served by `provider` for the extent of a continuation — the capability
the tools require (`with … credential`). Each ask resolves the provider's named credential through the
runtime (`oauth.token`): the runtime returns the stored token while its recorded lifetime holds and refreshes
it against the stored token endpoint once due, so no token bookkeeping lives in the program. The token is a
`string of private` — it flows only toward a submission sink (the `Bearer` header). A credential that needs a
human (never authorized, or refresh-dead) never throws: the ask PARKS the run on a `prelude.oauth.authorize`
escalation and resumes once the browser flow completes. A transient resolution failure throws
`oauth.server_error` at the provider.
declarations.name: credential
declarations.signature: request credential() -> string of private

declarations.checkedType: agent(continuation: agent(value: null) -> T0 with credential | E1, source: env | oauth) -> T0 with throw[missing_secret | server_error] | E1 | io
declarations.documentation:
Provide the Google credential for the extent of the continuation, from @source@ — the
credentials-unification shape: `use gmail.provider(source = credentials.oauth(name = "google"))`
(the same stored Google credential the `google_calendar` package uses, given a Gmail scope). Resolution
happens on EVERY `credential` ask (the runtime owns the token material, its cache and its refresh, so this
provider holds no secret and keeps no state); an unauthorized oauth credential parks the run on a
`prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation rather than failing, and a transient resolution failure throws at the
asking call.
declarations.name: provider
declarations.signature: agent provider[R, effect E](source: credentials.source, continuation: agent(value: null) -> R with {...E, credential}) -> R with E | io | prelude.throw[env.missing_secret | oauth.server_error]

declarations.checkedType: agent(body: unknown, context: string, method: string, url: string) -> unknown with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Issue an authenticated Gmail API call — @method@ to @url@ with @body@ (a value tree, or `null` for a
call carrying no document) — and return the reply parsed as JSON, or `null` for an empty one. Every
endpoint in this package goes through here. The `Bearer` header, the 2xx check and the classification are
`google_common.call`'s; what this adds is the ONE thing that is Gmail's, the `credential` ask, so no call
site has to spell it. A non-2xx becomes `google_common.classify_api_error(@context@, ...)` (401/403 →
`http.auth_error`, else `http.api_error`); @context@ names the caller for the message.
declarations.name: gmail_call

anyOf.description:
api_error: An authenticated API call failed for anything OTHER than the credential: a non-2xx @status@ that is not
401/403 — a malformed request, a resource that is not there, a rate limit, a server error. Nothing about
the caller's identity is in question, so backing off and replaying the call AS IT STANDS is the whole
recovery for the transient half, and the other half (a 400 the service is simply refusing) will keep
failing until the ARGUMENT changes.

WHICH half a given failure is, is read off @status@ and nowhere else: 408 / 429 / 5xx are the transient
ones a retry policy should back off and repeat, every other status is a refusal that will repeat forever.
That is the whole reason the status RIDES on the error instead of being folded into a sentence — a retry
policy downstream reads a number, never a message.

@context@ says WHICH call failed in the caller's own words; @message@ carries the server's own body
verbatim, because it is the diagnosis and a model handed this error reads it and adjusts.

anyOf.description:

403 — so the CREDENTIAL is what failed: revoked, expired past what its holder believed, or scoped too
narrowly for this call. Retrying with the SAME credential cannot succeed; the recovery is a fresh
RESOLUTION of it, which is why the ordinary composition is a `supervise` converter that signals
`supervise.interrupted`: the re-run resolves the credential again, and one the runtime cannot refresh parks
the run on a `prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation — a human's re-authorization prompt — rather than
failing. That is the whole line this variant draws: an `auth_error` may need a HUMAN before any retry can
work, an `api_error` never does.

(403 is read as auth even though some APIs also spend it on quota exhaustion. The access-rejection reading
is the one worth composing a re-resolution around, and a quota 403 that is replayed simply fails again.)

declarations.documentation:
Every attachment Gmail reports under a @payload@, walking `parts` to any depth — a `multipart/mixed`
message keeps its files next to a nested `multipart/alternative` text, and a forwarded mail nests deeper
still. The test is the one the API itself makes: a part whose `body.attachmentId` is present is a part
whose bytes Gmail is holding for a separate fetch, so it is listed, while a part carrying inline
`body.data` (the text of the mail) is not. Total — a payload with neither an attachment id nor parts
yields the empty list. Internal to `render_message` and `fetch_attachment`.

Tool: read a message's body by @id@. Returns the body as a `message_body` — the @text@ and the
@content_type@ of the part it came from — so a reader always knows WHAT it is holding. The preference is
`text/plain` (the `payload.body.data`, or for a `multipart/*` message the first `text/plain` descendant's,
base64url-decoded to real text); a message with no plain-text part anywhere — an HTML-only mail, which a
newsletter, a receipt and most mail a company sends all are — comes back with @content_type@

reads perfectly well, whereas nothing at all would report a full message as blank. Expect tags in that
case, and expect a long HTML mail to be a long result. A message with neither part comes back with
@content_type@ `null` and Gmail's SNIPPET — the short plain-text preview the API carries on every
resource — so the read is never empty-handed. ATTACHMENTS are not part of the body: they are listed on the
`message` (`list_recent`) and fetched by `fetch_attachment`.

declarations.documentation:
Tool: fetch ONE of a message's attachments and return it as a file. @id@ is the MESSAGE's id (a
`list_recent` result's @id@ — not its @message_id@) and @attachment_id@ is the @attachment_id@ of one entry
in that message's @attachments@ list. PASS @content_type@ TOO — the very `content_type` that listing showed
beside the attachment_id. Gmail regenerates attachment ids on every message read, so when this agent has to
re-read the message to look the type up itself, the id you hold may no longer match any part and the file
comes back UNTYPED — a receiver then sees a generic `.bin` it cannot preview. The listing in your hands is
the reliable source; the re-read is only the fallback when you omit it. The result is a `file` handle: the
bytes stay runtime-side, so the handle can be passed straight on to any other tool you hold that takes a
file — a viewer to LOOK at it, or an outbound tool's files to send it onward — while the payload itself
never enters the conversation. (The file carries a TYPE but no NAME yet, so a receiver sees a generated
name like `file-1.pdf`; say the real filename in your message when it matters.) This only READS: nothing in
the mailbox changes, and one call fetches one attachment, so ask for the one you actually need. A payload
that comes back corrupt throws `files.malformed_base64` rather than handing back broken bytes; a non-2xx
reply raises `http.api_failure` (`http.auth_error` | `http.api_error`).

declarations.documentation:
Tool: send a plain-text email from the authenticated user. @to@ is the recipient address, @subject@ the
subject line, @body@ the message body. Returns the sent message's id. To REPLY inside a conversation, pass
@thread_id@ (a message's `thread_id`, so Gmail files the reply in that thread) and @in_reply_to@ (the

headers, so a mail client threads it too. (Compose the @subject@ yourself — prefix "Re: " for a reply.)

`http.api_failure` (`http.auth_error` | `http.api_error`) on a non-2xx reply.

declarations.documentation:
Every message id matching @query@, across ALL result pages, OLDEST FIRST — `watch`'s per-poll listing.
@page_token@ is `null` for the first page and @accumulated@ the ids gathered so far. Draining every page
is what `poll.subscribe` requires of a `fetch` and what makes its cursor safe: Gmail lists matches NEWEST
first and offers no ascending order, so a listing cut off at a cap would hand back the newest matches only,
and a cursor advanced over them would strand the older ones below it forever. The recursion depth is the
number of pages in ONE poll (500 matches a page — a poll's arrivals, not the mailbox), not the daemon's
lifetime, so it does not accumulate like a per-tick loop would. Internal to `watch`.

declarations.checkedType: agent(cursor_at: fresh | resume, deliver_to: agent(value: message) -> null with E2, poll_interval_milliseconds: number, query: string) -> never with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | get | set | E2 | io
declarations.documentation:
Watch the mailbox for mail that ARRIVES matching a Gmail search @query@ and deliver each new message
once, oldest first, to @deliver_to@ — `poll.subscribe` under a Gmail adapter, so it composes under
`parallel [ … ]` beside any other daemon and never resolves (`-> never`). Every
@poll_interval_milliseconds@ it searches `<@query@> after:<cursor>` (@query@ is the ordinary Gmail search
language — "is:unread", "from:alice@example.com"), hands each unseen message to @deliver_to@, and moves
the cursor to that message's own arrival instant (Gmail's `internalDate`, never the poller's clock).
@deliver_to@'s effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged, so a delivery may itself call other
tools (reply, label).

DELIVERY IS AT-LEAST-ONCE — `poll.subscribe`'s contract, in its words. A message reaches @deliver_to@ one
or more times, never zero: the commit lands only after a delivery returns, so a crash or a throw in between
re-delivers exactly that message on the next tick. EXACTLY-ONCE IS BUILT AT THE DESTINATION, by making the
delivery idempotent — key it on the `message`'s @id@, which is the identity this subscription already
promises is stable — never by expecting the loop to be stronger than the mailbox allows.

@cursor_at@ DECIDES WHAT A RESTART DOES, and it is the consequential choice here. `poll.resume(key = ...)`
keeps the cursor in the store, so a runtime restart, a re-forked fiber and a `replay` re-run all resume
from it and the mail that arrived while the watch was DOWN is delivered, oldest first, on the tick after it
comes back. `poll.fresh()` keeps the cursor in the run alone: every fresh activation re-primes at that
moment and the downtime is skipped for good, silently. There is no default — a watch that will be re-forked
(a persisted monitor, anything under `replay`) wants `resume` with a key of its own, and a second watch
sharing one key overwrites the first's cursor.

WHAT IT REPORTS IS ARRIVAL, NOT MATCHING. The mail already in the mailbox when the subscription first
starts is never delivered, however well it matches: a watch started on "is:unread" over 200 unread
messages stays silent until the next mail arrives. By the same token, mail that comes to match @query@
LATER — an old message you star, label or mark unread — is not delivered either, because the search never
looks below the cursor. This is the right shape for hearing about incoming mail, and the wrong one for a
general "tell me whenever anything matches this search" trigger; `list_recent` answers the latter. (The
`after:` boundary's granularity is one second, and the subscription re-lists a second's worth below its
cursor on every tick — so a message at the cursor's own second is listed again and deduplicated by its id,
not delivered twice.)

No retry is built in — a poll failure (an http error, a rejected token, a @deliver_to@ that throws)
propagates and kills the subscription, exactly as an uncaught failure in any callee does. Compose
resilience by wrapping the watch in a replay provider (`replay.forever` with a converter that replays the
transient blips AND `http.auth_error` — the re-run re-resolves the token, and a credential needing a human
parks on the runtime's authorize escalation rather than failing). With @cursor_at@ = `poll.resume(...)` the
backoff costs nothing but latency: the cursor outlives the failed activation, so the mail that arrived
during it is delivered once the watch is back. The first poll is one @poll_interval_milliseconds@ in (a
`time.watch` occurrence fires one interval after the start), so a message arriving just after the watch
starts waits up to one interval — it is not lost, only pending.
